specPoints.text: describe the dangers of ionising radiations, including: • that radiation can cause mutations in living organisms • that radiation can damage cells and tissue • the problems arising from the disposal of radioactive waste and how the associated risks can be reduced

primer.text: Ionising radiation damages cells: DNA breaks, repairs fail, mutations and cancer follow. Which radiation is worst depends on geography — alpha inside, gamma outside. Handling rules, dosemeter badges and engineered waste disposal keep the dose ledger short.

lessons.title: Ionisation inside the body and out
sourceHeadings: Effect of radiation on a living cell
lessons.opening: All ionising radiations can damage cells and tissue and cause mutations that lead to cancer. Inside the body, the strongly ionising alpha is the most dangerous; outside it, the deeply penetrating gamma is worst — alpha can barely reach the skin from the air.
keyPoints: Ionising radiation can cause mutations in living organisms.
It can damage cells and tissue, sometimes leading to cancer.
Inside the body, alpha is the most harmful because it is the most ionising.
Outside the body, gamma is the most harmful because it is the most penetrating.
Gamma ionises about 20 times less than alpha per interaction, but reaches where alpha cannot.

low.restatement: Inside: alpha is a wrecker up close (swallowed source). Outside: alpha stops in air, gamma goes straight to your cells.
low.analogy: Alpha is a boxer — devastating in the ring, harmless from the street; gamma is a sniper’s torch — weak touch, long reach.
low.examPointer: The in/out inversion is the exam favourite: alpha worst inside, gamma worst outside. Justify both with ionising vs penetrating.

medium.restatement: Tissue damage begins with DNA ionisation: breaks usually repair, but mis-repair fixes a mutation, and cumulative mutations raise cancer risk. Radiation type ranks harm through two independent axes — ionisation density (inside) and range (outside) — so hazard assessments must fix the geometry first.
medium.analogy: Harm ranking is like ranking vehicles: a lorry (alpha) is deadliest in a crowded room, a motorway (gamma) carries danger to the far horizon.
medium.examPointer: Mutations + cell/tissue damage + waste disposal — the three-part list of spec 7.16. Hit all three in long answers.

check.stem: Which radiation is most dangerous if a source is swallowed?

options.explanation: Alpha’s strong ionisation acts directly on internal tissue.

check.stem: Which radiation is most dangerous when the source is outside the body?

options.explanation: Gamma penetrates skin and reaches internal cells.
Alpha is absorbed by air before the skin.
Beta penetrates moderately, less than gamma.

check.stem: How can ionising radiation damage a living cell?

options.text: it ionises DNA; mis-repair of the damage can fix a mutation
it feeds the cell extra energy

check.stem: Why is alpha nearly harmless from an external source a metre away?

options.text: its range in air is only a few centimetres
options.explanation: Alpha cannot reach the body from a metre.

options.text: air destroys the alpha particles’ nature
options.explanation: Absorption by range, not destruction of identity.

check.stem: A worker ingests equal activities of an alpha emitter and a gamma emitter. Which causes more localised harm, and why?

options.text: the alpha emitter — its dense ionisation acts directly on internal organs
options.explanation: Internal geometry favours the strong ioniser.

options.text: the gamma emitter — it penetrates the organs best

options.explanation: Internal emitters are the classic hazard.

check.stem: State two dangers of ionising radiation to living organisms.
check.modelAnswer: Radiation can cause mutations in living organisms and can damage cells and tissue.

check.stem: Which radiation is most harmful inside the body, and which outside?
check.modelAnswer: Alpha is the most harmful inside the body (most ionising); gamma is the most harmful outside (most penetrating).

check.stem: Explain the reversal: alpha is worst inside the body but nearly harmless outside.
check.modelAnswer: Alpha’s intense ionisation does maximal damage where it lands, so inside the body it harms organs directly; outside, its few-centimetre range in air means it never reaches the skin, while gamma’s long range carries its weaker ionisation deep into the body.

check.stem: A hospital stores two sources: an alpha emitter and a gamma emitter, both sealed. Which storage demands thicker shielding, and why?
check.modelAnswer: The gamma emitter: gamma is the most penetrating, so lead-lined thick shielding is needed; alpha is contained by almost any solid and even by a few centimetres of air.

lessons.title: Safe handling and waste disposal
lessons.opening: Hands stay safe with shielded storage, tongs, protective clothing and short exposure times, while dosemeter badges keep a running dose record. Waste is sorted by its emission — alpha in canisters, beta in metal plus concrete, gamma in lead-lined silos — and long-lived waste is buried deep and dry.
keyPoints: Keep sources in shielded, lead-lined containers when not in use.
Handle sources with gloves and tongs, and limit the time a source is out.
A dosemeter (or radiation badge) records a worker’s accumulated dose.
Waste storage escalates with penetration: plastic/metal canisters for alpha, metal plus concrete for beta, lead-lined thick concrete for gamma.
Long-half-life waste is buried underground in geologically stable, secure sites to protect groundwater.

low.restatement: Lab rules: lead box, tongs, short visits, badge on the chest. Waste rules: match the container to the radiation, bury the long-lived stuff deep and dry.
low.analogy: The badge is a odometer for dose — it never blocks the miles, it just records them.
low.examPointer: List-four safety questions: lead-lined storage, tongs, distance, minimal time (plus hand-washing) — give several, not one.

medium.restatement: Dose monitoring converts an invisible hazard into a measured quantity that can be capped by rostering; waste engineering, meanwhile, matches barriers to penetration and adds time as a barrier — geological isolation, corrosion-resistant containers and site stability guard the very long half-lives against groundwater pathways.
medium.analogy: Waste disposal is a multi-lock vault: the right metal for the radiation, concrete and lead as walls, and geology as the moat — for centuries.
medium.examPointer: Waste answers score by matching emitter to container: alpha→canister, beta→metal+concrete, gamma→lead-lined concrete. Memorise the trio.

check.stem: What does a dosemeter badge do?

options.text: records the accumulated radiation dose a worker receives
options.explanation: The badge is the dose ledger.

options.text: shields the worker from gamma rays
options.explanation: It monitors, it does not shield.

check.stem: Why must burial sites for long-lived waste be geologically stable?

options.text: earthquakes or ground movement could breach containers and release waste into groundwater
options.explanation: Stability protects the containment over centuries.
Geology does not change decay rates.
Disposal is not meant to be easy retrieval.

check.stem: Which practice belongs to safe handling of sources?

options.text: using tongs and keeping the source in a lead-lined box when idle
holding the source in a bare hand briefly
storing it on the open bench overnight
pointing it at colleagues for checks

check.stem: Rust and corrosion resistance matter for waste containers because…

options.text: containers must stay intact for very long periods in hostile conditions
options.explanation: Integrity over centuries is the design brief.
Chemistry does not change nuclear activity.

check.stem: List four precautions a student should take when using a radioactive source.
check.modelAnswer: Store the source in its lead-lined box until the moment it is needed, handle it with tongs, keep maximum distance, and minimise the time it is out (then wash hands and log the usage).

check.stem: Match each waste type to its storage: alpha, beta, gamma emitters.
check.modelAnswer: Alpha waste in plastic or metal canisters; beta waste in metal canisters inside concrete silos; gamma waste in lead-lined, thick concrete silos.

check.stem: Explain why sources with long half-lives shape the whole waste-disposal problem.
check.modelAnswer: Long half-lives keep the waste radioactive and dangerous for very long times, so containers must resist corrosion and sites must stay stable and secure for centuries to keep it out of groundwater.

check.stem: A radiographer’s quarterly badge reading has crept upward across the year. Give two system changes that would reduce the dose.
check.modelAnswer: Reduce exposure time per procedure (roster or automation) and increase distance/shielding — for example remote handling or better screens — so the recorded dose per quarter falls.

glossary.definition: A permanent change to DNA that can follow ionising damage and mis-repair.
A worn device (or badge) that records the radiation dose a person receives.
Material emitting ionising radiation that must be stored or disposed of securely.
Water beneath the ground that buried waste must never contaminate.
